definitions.meaning: A boundary where two plates move towards each other.
A plate of thin but dense rock that sits low, carrying ocean above it.
A plate of thicker but lighter rock that rides higher and carries land.
The sinking of the denser plate beneath the lighter plate at a convergent boundary.
The deep fold at the surface where the sinking plate bends downwards.
The force of gravity on the cold, dense sinking slab, dragging the rest of the plate behind it.
A sudden shaking as rock cracks and grinds - here, fired along the path of the sinking slab.
Molten rock below the surface, formed here when the slab releases water that melts the mantle above it.
A curved line of volcanoes built by rising magma on the overriding plate, parallel to the trench.
The hot, slowly flowing rock beneath the plates, into which the slab sinks.

mechanismSteps: Convergence: an oceanic plate and a continental plate move towards each other, and the oceanic plate is denser (s1).
The bend: the leading edge of the oceanic plate bends downwards, and the deep fold is the ocean trench (s2).
Slab-pull: the heavy sinking slab is dragged down by gravity and pulls the rest of the plate behind it, while earthquakes fire along its path (s3).
The arc: the slab heats up, releases water that melts the mantle above it, and rising magma builds a volcanic arc parallel to the trench (s4).
objectives: Describe subduction at a convergent boundary between an oceanic and a continental plate
Explain slab-pull as the force that drives the sinking plate
Link the trench, earthquakes and volcanic arc into one causal chain
subject: geography
title: Subduction: slab-pull, trench and volcanic arc

trap.explanation: The slip: The overriding plate looks bigger and stronger, so it seems to do the pushing. The fix: Nothing pushes it down: the cold, dense slab sinks under its own weight - slab-pull - and drags the rest of the plate behind it. In class, replay scene 3: freeze the slab deep below the surface and ask what could still be pushing it there - nothing touches it, yet it keeps sinking and pulling.
trap.misconception: The continental plate pushes the oceanic plate down underneath it.

workedExample: Test the push claim on the sinking slab. Step 1 (s2): the oceanic plate bends down at the trench under its own density. Step 2 (s3): far below the surface, beyond any contact push, the slab keeps sinking - its weight produces slab-pull that drags the plate behind it. So the driver is slab-pull, not a push from the continental plate.
